name: Jamal Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say here is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee driller at Mount Corrie, an open-pit gold mine. I run a blast hole rig, which drills rows of holes, say twelve metres deep, in a set pattern, and then the shot crew fills them with explosives. My day is lining up on each hole off the GPS, drilling, logging what the ground felt like, and moving to the next one. I'm on maybe a hundred and twenty holes a shift on a good day; the experienced blokes do a lot more.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you to the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My knees. I was a carpenter for twenty years, mostly house frames, and by forty my knees sounded like bubble wrap every morning. A drill rig has a good seat. My wife Grace works at a bank branch in town, and we've got Theo, fifteen, and Mia, eleven. We've got savings, and a block of land out past the showgrounds that I always meant to build our house on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's precise, like carpentry: if your holes are out, the blast is out, and everybody knows it was you. What's hard is I'm still learning to read the ground. My supervisor Anneke can tell by the sound of the rig whether it's hit a soft patch. I can't yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it was overhyped, like most things. I'd say it to the crew at crib and leave it there. I'm not much for online arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's simple, I get to keep learning and moving up. I'd like to be the one who hears the soft ground by sound in a couple of years. That's all I really want from this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Keep saving, maybe start drawing up plans for the house on the block. I already use one of those AI apps now and then to price materials, so I'd keep doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI to price materials. How did you start with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace's work brought it in for writing letters, and she showed me. I used to spend Sunday nights with a calculator and a timber catalogue, and now it takes me ten minutes. That's the kind of AI I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Grace say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, I think. Her branch has been talking about chatbots taking over the counter for two years. If it's mostly hype, she keeps her job and we keep things as they are.

S0.say: He'd tell the crew at crib that it was overhyped, like most things. He'd leave it there and stay out of online arguments.
S0.think: He'd be glad to keep learning and moving up, hoping to read soft ground by sound within a couple of years.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving, starts drawing up plans for the house on their block of land, and keeps using AI occasionally to price materials.
S0.quote: I used to spend Sunday nights with a calculator and a timber catalogue, and now it takes me ten minutes.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal sees AI as a handy tool when it saves his Sunday nights, not as a threat. His wife's bank job is a second exposure point he keeps an eye on. His goals are modest and craft-centred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change and we'll work through it, like the GPS when it came in. I'd say the company and government both need to play fair with notice and training. I'm not a big blamer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, drill rigs are one of the first things going automatic. I've seen a rig at another site drilling a whole pattern with nobody in it. I picked this job for the seat, and it turns out the seat is what they're getting rid of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what happened to the drillers at the sites that switched first. If they moved into supervising the automatic rigs, I'd ask for that training in the first year. Meanwhile I'd keep the savings safe and maybe do some weekend carpentry, small jobs, to keep my hand in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see the problem, but I can also see a couple of ways around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep your hand in at carpentry. Is that a backup plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of. My knees can do decks and pergolas, just not full frames. If the mine went sour, I could do small jobs around town and not be starving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anneke, funnily enough. She's the best driller on site, and in this picture her skill is exactly the thing that gets built into the machine. The rig learns to listen to the ground like she does.

S1.say: He'd say it's a change to work through, like GPS when it arrived, and that companies and government both need to play fair with notice and training.
S1.think: He knows drill rigs are among the first to go automatic and finds it ironic that the seat he chose for his knees is what's being removed.
S1.do: Watches how drillers at early-switching sites fare, asks for supervision training in the first year if it works out, keeps savings safe, and takes small weekend carpentry jobs.
S1.feel: Uneasy but able to see ways around it.
S1.quote: I picked this job for the seat, and it turns out the seat is what they're getting rid of.
S1.fieldNote: Jamal's steady nature shows: he watches others first, then moves. His carpentry gives him a real backup he trusts. He worries for his skilled supervisor, whose ear for the ground is exactly what the machine would copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving too fast and someone should hit the brakes, though I don't know who. I'd say both governments and companies should slow it down until people can catch up. Probably all I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, both our jobs go: my drilling and Grace's bank job. And with robots doing hands-on work, my carpentry backup goes too. That's the first picture that properly scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Grace that first weekend and look at everything: savings, the land, the mortgage. I think we'd sell the block while land's still worth something and put it on the mortgage. I'd keep working to the last day and stop all big spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Proper worried, but we'd have a plan and some money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years' warning change things compared with none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time to sell the block properly and not in a panic. That's about it. You can't build a new career in two years, but you can tidy up your money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling the block means giving up the house you meant to build. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the end of something. I've been building that house in my head for ten years. I'd have to let a robot build someone else's instead. But a smaller mortgage beats a nice dream.

S2.say: He'd say it's moving too fast and someone should slow it down, though he doesn't know who, and that governments and companies share responsibility.
S2.think: He sees both his and his wife's jobs going, plus his carpentry backup, which makes this the first scenario that really scares him.
S2.do: Reviews savings, land and mortgage with his wife the first weekend, sells their block of land to pay down the mortgage, works to the last day and stops big spending.
S2.feel: Anxious and worried, but with a plan and some money.
S2.quote: I've been building that house in my head for ten years. I'd have to let a robot build someone else's instead.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Jamal's backups fall away at once: his trade, his drilling and his wife's job. His response is orderly, focused on money rather than careers. Giving up the dream house on the block is the painful heart of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get things sorted if people start now. I'd say the company should be training us for whatever's left, and the government should make sure they do. Sensible stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is about the length of my learning curve. By the time I'm actually good at drilling, the rig won't need me. That's a bit funny, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and saving. In year one or two, once I saw what jobs were surviving, I'd move. I think I'd look at being a maintenance fitter's offsider on the automatic rigs, because they'll still need fixing for a while. I'd also build a small unit on the block to rent out, so there's rent coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most of the time, anxious when I think about Theo finishing school into that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why build a rental rather than sell the block, like in the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because five years is enough time to build. I'm a carpenter, I can do most of it myself on weekends. Rent comes in whether a robot's driving the rig or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Theo, finishing school around then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to pick something he likes and be ready to change it. I changed at forty. He's a smart kid, he'll work it out quicker than I did.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough if people start now, with companies training workers and government making sure they do.
S3.think: He notes wryly that his learning curve and the five-year window are the same length, so he'd be good just as the rig stops needing him.
S3.do: Keeps drilling and saving, moves in year one or two to a maintenance offsider role on automatic rigs, and builds a small rental unit on his block on weekends.
S3.feel: Mostly uneasy, anxious when thinking of his son leaving school.
S3.quote: Rent comes in whether a robot's driving the rig or not.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns the block of land from something to sell into something to build on. Jamal's carpentry becomes an asset rather than a backup. His worry moves to his eldest son, which he handles with practical advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is good notice and nobody should be caught out. I'd tell the younger blokes to use it. I'd also say the government needs a plan for people who can't retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine, I reckon. Ten years and I'd have a paid-off house, maybe the rental, and the kids nearly grown. My worry would be Grace, because she's less keen on change than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build the house on the block properly, slowly, over three or four years, and rent out the old one. Keep drilling while it lasts and get my maintenance tickets around year four. Help Grace find a course if her branch starts closing, maybe something in aged care where she can still talk to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit uneasy for Grace, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change most compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The block. With two years I sell my dream to pay the bank. With ten I build it and rent out the old house. Same man, same robot, very different ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned worrying about Grace. Have you talked to her about any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not properly. She changes the subject. I'd probably bring it up on one of our walks, when the kids aren't around. That's when we talk about the big things.

S4.say: He'd call ten years good notice, tell younger workers to use it, and say the government needs a plan for people who can't retrain.
S4.think: He thinks he'd be fine with a paid-off house, maybe a rental, and grown kids, but worries about his wife, who's less keen on change.
S4.do: Builds the house on the block over three or four years and rents out the old one, keeps drilling while it lasts, gets maintenance tickets around year four, and helps his wife find a course if her branch closes.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, a bit uneasy for his wife.
S4.quote: With two years I sell my dream to pay the bank. With ten I build it and rent out the old house.
S4.fieldNote: The decade lets Jamal keep the dream house and add rental income. His concern shifts almost entirely to his wife. He talks about big things on walks, which suggests a careful, private approach to family worries.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Grace's job, my job and my trade all go at once. What would help is the company giving proper notice and some money to retrain, and the government making sure people over forty don't just get forgotten.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask how people decide things with their partners. Most of us aren't deciding alone. Half my plans depend on whether Grace's bank still has a counter, and nobody asks about her.

headlineQuote: Half my plans depend on whether Grace's bank still has a counter, and nobody asks about her.
portrait: Jamal Walsh is a 43-year-old trainee blast hole driller at an open-pit gold mine, who moved over after twenty years of carpentry wore out his knees. He's married to a bank branch worker, has two kids, solid savings and a block of land where he's long dreamed of building. He's pragmatic, doesn't blame any one side, and uses AI now and then for practical jobs. He watches others before moving, stays calm or uneasy in most scenarios, and becomes anxious only with two-year AGI, when he'd sell the block to clear the mortgage.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because his job, his wife's job and his carpentry trade would all go at once.
whatWouldHelp: Proper notice and retraining money from the company, and a government that makes sure people over forty aren't forgotten.
